entries.title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
entries.summary: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. entries.content:
If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life.

AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant.

Most of all, if you were a would-be autocrat, you would love the way that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini have thrown a grenade into thousands of years of teaching and learning: the way they threaten to upend our ability to think with the robust clarity that is needed in emergencies of justice. I write fiction for children and I hold a fellowship at Oxford University, so I spend a lot of time working with, and for, young people. I’ve seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives. I’ve seen, at the same time, how it has thrown stark and urgent light on how fundamental books and reading are to our shared understanding of who we are, and to our democracy.

There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.

Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.

Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.

Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.

AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.

At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread. Sewell Setzer III was 14 when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.

The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.

At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.

Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his Substack Systematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”

Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as a product. It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.

But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AI badly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.

What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”

I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing. To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.

There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.

I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.

So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.

There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us. Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.

entries.title: It’s not just Homer: the new generation of poets enjoying epic success
entries.summary: Christopher Nolan’s film has made the Odyssey a bestselling book again, but a slew of new poets are breaking sales records, and have more in common with the ancient Greek than you might expectThe death of poetry – much anticipated, much prematurely mourned – has been put off again, this time by the Odyssey. Thanks to Christopher Nolan’s film, sales of Homer’s epic rose 1,400% in the weeks around r
entries.content:
The death of poetry – much anticipated, much prematurely mourned – has been put off again, this time by the Odyssey. Thanks to Christopher Nolan’s film, sales of Homer’s epic rose 1,400% in the weeks around release – and it’s not alone. Poetry collections are once again sailing up the charts: Lucas Jones, Donna Ashworth and Nikita Gill, among others, have all burst forth on to the bestseller lists.

The word bestseller, it must be said, conjures up certain images: a TV tie-in cookbook; a sexy thriller. It does not, generally speaking, imply poetry. Poetry is a genre more often relegated to the adolescent, the academic, or the words inside sentimental birthday cards: either over-emotional or elitist, depending on which poet and which perspective. What it certainly is not is a money-spinner: nobody gets into poetry to make the big bucks. Nobody gets into poetry – not these days, anyway, not since Byron’s day – for the fame or the fortune.

Poetry is the underdog of publishing and yet this year, according to a recent Guardian article, it is “expected to exceed £15m in annual sales for the first time since records began”; it might even, if the Greek epics continue to pull in readers (as they have for almost 3,000 years), climb to an astounding £17m. Even without the bolstering influence of Homer, poetry has been steadily climbing for the last three years, each one the best on record.

In fact, reports of poetry’s surprising rise have been kicking around for more than a decade: Rupi Kaur’s million-dollar debut, Milk and Honey, set new records in 2014, and continues to sell. US magazine The New Republic named Kaur the “writer of the decade”. And yet she came to stand not so much for great art, as for a kind of synecdoche for what was wrong with art: Kaur became the mockable face of “the new poetry”, Instagrammable and Instagrammed, and accessed primarily – of course – by the young.

A new audience is finding poetry, particularly (though not exclusively) through social media: a new generation of poets, particularly but not exclusively performance poets, have come to prominence through Instagram, TikTok, and other short-form video formats. These writers, while we can quote them on the page, lose something by being written down.

“At my funeral I’d like there to be sunflowers, a truly inconvenient amount / For I too will have spent a lifetime searching for the light,” runs a couplet from Harry Baker’s Sunflowers, but the poet’s charismatic presence somehow conveys something more of the full power of his meaning.

Many of these poems, beginning on social media and ending in huge sold-out tours, rely on a connection between speaker and listener: a pause, a stillness, a sustained thread in the chaos of the internet, of singular attention to one poem through to the end.

This is poetry for the social media age, for sure. But then, what is the Odyssey except social media? The Odyssey is meant to be read out loud; to be told; to be spread; to be shared. What we know as a single written text is, in fact, only the most static, frozen form of the original viral myth.

It is tempting to think of these bestsellers as a new kind of poetry, but it is in fact a very old one. It is unafraid of emotion, of sentimentality, of faith and love; it is concerned less with the establishment of a brand new voice than with the need to give voice to a collective thought. It is not about originality. (Hence, perhaps, the accusations of self-help; banality; and even plagiarism that have been flung at some of these newly popular poets.) These are poems designed to resonate rather than to disturb. In times of division, these poems are made to connect.

All writing is about connection, even when it’s not. But the immediacy of the connection between author and reader is somehow easiest in poetry: when it works, there’s a direct shot to the heart, a human-to-human hot-wiring together that compresses time and space to get to the point.

What social media offers these poets is a new way to gather people round the fire – and, for some, a way to get to be the one speaking at last. If poets can reach their audiences directly, then different poets may be, perhaps, given a chance not just to speak but to be heard: working-class poets, queer poets, poets who don’t fit the “male, pale and stale” classical canon.

This is how poetry thrives. Poetry needs the new so that it can keep on telling the oldest stories we have: love, despair, grief, hope, joy, community, companionship. Long may it live – as thrilling as every other bestseller on the charts.

Five bestselling poets you should know about

Lucas Jones: actor, TikTok star, bestselling poet

Writes about: masculinity, faith, life, death and love

From I Saw God on the Train, from the new collection I Still Believe In Miracles:

You want white clouds and endless skies? Err, yeah. Look around. You don’t have to die […]

I know it probably brings you some pain

to think of the dead as just dust in a grave […] Life is the cloud, and death is the rain.

Hollie McNish: winner of the Ted Hughes prize, author of Slug, Lobster, Virgin, Plum and Nobody Told Me

Writes about: sex, motherhood, longing, politics, power and love

From call me:

call me

even if you’re in the wrong place at the wrong time

with a full moon and a lone wolf whimpering bloody-pawed from your insides

[...]

i do not care what you have done … i am no god i am no judge

i am your mother – call me and i will come

Nikita Gill: permanently on the bestseller chart, 850,000 Instagram followers

Writes about: feminist-flavoured myths, magic, legends and love

93% Stardust:

We have calcium in our bones,

iron in our veins,

carbon in our souls,

and nitrogen in our brains.

93 percent stardust,

with souls made of flames,

we are all just stars

that have people names.

Lemn Sissay: Sunday Times bestseller, OBE, books include Let the Light Pour In

Writes about: family, adoption, the fabric of society, race, home, hope, and love

From Let the Light Pour In:

If the phone won’t ring make the call

If the mountain won’t move shift it

If the birds won’t sing, sing to them all,

And if the sun won’t rise, lift it

Len Pennie: British book award winner, Scots language poet also writing in English

Writes about: language, linguistics, shame, stigma, suffering, surviving, the patriarchy, overthrowing the patriarchy and love

From The Vow, from Poyums Annaw:

To be loved through each compromise, question or qualm

To be sheltered from storm and

enshrined in the calm

To be held, not like glass, but the end of a deal …

entries.title: What Happened to Liberal Democracy? by Daron Acemoglu review – how to fix the system
entries.summary: The Nobel-winning economist takes aim at elites for no longer meeting the needs of the massesIn 2009, the tech billionaire Peter Thiel published an essay with the portentous title The Education of a Libertarian, in which he announced: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” Since the 1920s, he wrote, “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the fran
entries.content:
In 2009, the tech billionaire Peter Thiel published an essay with the portentous title The Education of a Libertarian, in which he announced: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” Since the 1920s, he wrote, “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” had rendered the notion of “capitalist democracy” an oxymoron. To be fair, Thiel still seems happy to exercise his freedom to extract money from democracies, via his co-founding of Palantir, which was lately given lots of money by the NHS.

Thiel calls himself, as many such do, a “classical liberal”, but Daron Acemoglu argues that his ilk still has much in common with left-liberals. All of them, he writes, agree on “the desirability of basic individual rights and freedoms (including the right not to be coerced and the freedoms of expression, religion, association, and choice); constraints on power, especially political power; and broad protections for equality before the law”. On his telling, by the mid-20th century democracy with liberal characteristics had amply proved its worth: blue-collar labour was generously rewarded, and there was a sense of “shared prosperity”.

But now, he argues, liberal democracy is in a crisis, largely owing to the abandonment of the working class by liberalism’s “progressive” wing. In post-industrial Europe and the US, the left ceased to speak of economic class and spoke instead of identity. It is a similar diagnosis to that offered by the French sociologist Didier Eribon in his Retour à Reims, and indeed by Bernie Sanders, who has spoken of “a Democratic party which has abandoned working-class people”, but Acemoglu is happier to wield culture-war rhetoric even as he deplores the culture wars. He accuses the left, for example, of being obsessed with both “social engineering” (via diversity initiatives) and “thought policing”, which is impossible (he means speech policing).

His solution is a new contract of “working-class liberal democracy”, which concentrates on improving the standard of living of the least educated or skilled. This is to be done by focusing on economic growth (reducing, for example, the regulatory hoops one must apparently jump through to become a hairdresser or a masseur), encouraging more community decision-making (possibly imitating the citizens’ assemblies used in the Republic of Ireland), and making social media companies responsible, as publishers, for the messages they promote to users (good luck!). He suggests legislating in favour of “worker AI”, by which employees could use expert systems based on machine-learning to help them be more productive, so that nurses, for instance, could take more medical decisions. (He doesn’t report having consulted doctors on this idea.)

Acemoglu is a smooth and intelligent writer, and there is much in here to fascinate, particularly when he is on home turf: there is a brilliant explanation of why the American tax code perversely incentivises automation and job destruction, and how the enviable happiness of Norway and Sweden, far from being a result of some innate Nordic wisdom, followed deliberate economic reforms enacted as recently as the 1930s. He is also laudably ready to admit when there is no “ready-made answer” to liberalism’s tensions – between, say, a value of community cohesion and a value of welcoming others who are different.

But his expansive rhetoric does lead to some internal inconsistencies. Acemoglu denounces throughout the progressive-liberal elites in exactly the same way as modern populists do (Farage-like, he even says liberalism’s troubles have reached “boiling point”). Yet, having eased the reader through a potted history of the ideas of Rousseau, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Kant, Voltaire et al, he concedes that liberalism itself was the invention of a small bunch of clever people: “an ideology created by a highly learned group of philosophers”. So maybe elites are good, sometimes? And Acemoglu can hardly escape the charge that his own book – one written by a Nobel-winning economist, no less – is itself an example of the kind of top-down “elite debates” he claims to think are sterile. Nor should he try to, because the charge would be stupid; indeed, the kind of thing that an elite billionaire like Peter Thiel would say.

entries.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
entries.summary: The Salt King by Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN VairThe Salt King by by Natasha Pulley (Gollancz, £22)The latest from the author of The Watchmaker of Filigree Street blends an apocalyptic end-of-the-world tale with folk horror and two slowly developing love stories. Avelyn Brocken is a trainee priest at the Vatican, sent to check o
entries.content:
The Salt King by by Natasha Pulley (Gollancz, £22)

The latest from the author of The Watchmaker of Filigree Street blends an apocalyptic end-of-the-world tale with folk horror and two slowly developing love stories. Avelyn Brocken is a trainee priest at the Vatican, sent to check out a possible miracle in the fens of East Anglia. His only qualification for the job is that he was born and raised in Hreodwater, a strange community based around a salt mine with its own language, religion and rituals. But what begins in Hreodwater, involving the mysterious salt light and a sleeping king deep in the mine, threatens civilisations. An original, rich and gripping tale that’s also an interesting exploration of the power of faith.

A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett (Hodderscape, £25)

A new case for Ana and Din, the crime-solving team introduced in the Hugo and World Fantasy award-winning novel The Tainted Cup, focuses on a murder among the cattle-ranching gentry of the Empire of Khanum. The murderer has been caught red-handed, unable to remember what happened. The victim was his lover, and their families were enemies; he is the last of his line, and fears his family is cursed. The detectives suspect a more material and dangerous adversary behind the scenes, with access to a terrifying weapon. This is the sort of other-world fantasy with close ties to speculative fiction, based on natural laws and science rather than any magical system, and some of the issues it raises are of immediate concern in today’s world of shrinking resources. Great world-building and a masterfully conceived mystery make for a compelling cross-genre blend.

Netherwood by Jake Arnott (Titan, £18.99)

London is too expensive, so artist Adam and his partner Justine buy a house in Hastings. The room at the top will make the perfect studio for Adam, whose career has stalled after drink, drugs and quarrels. They’re intrigued by the property’s “special feature” – a cave hidden behind a locked door in the back wall. After they move in they discover a Latin phrase carved into the wall, layers of candle wax, a mysterious sealed bottle: evidence of occult rituals? It turns out the previous owner was a devotee of chaos magic, inspired by the notorious Aleister Crowley, who died in a Hastings boarding house called Netherwood. Justine fears they could be in danger, sensing the ghostly presence of a frightened girl, but at the same time, their new home is inspiring Adam to create his most powerful paintings, winning back the support of his agent and the promise of big money. A wonderfully unnerving, evocative horror in which Hastings looms large as the most uncanny place in England.

Fawn by CN Vair (3AM, £20)

This debut begins with deceptive gentleness, introducing the reader to Tess, a witch in present-day America who sold her soul to the devil in 1935, the price for surviving a murderous attack. She hardly seems to have aged, but is careful to keep the locals from noticing, using spells to turn unwanted attention away and keep herself and her animal sanctuary safe. Things start to go wrong when she rescues a fawn, born at the wrong time of year with teeth and a thirst for blood. She ignores advice to put it down, but when the local cop insists it must be destroyed, and a new preacher arrives in town, seeming to turn her friends against her, she struggles to maintain control. Just when she needs them most, the old spells are failing her. Like a newborn fawn, she’s doomed to be seen as prey. Tess refuses to accept defeat, on any level; she will do whatever it takes to survive in this disturbing, seductively written fiction about power and female rage.

entries.title: Jason Arday claimed he was paid ‘1.4 million’ by publisher for memoir
entries.summary: Simon & Schuster still plans to publish book by Cambridge academic who resigned this week amid plagiarism claimsJason Arday, the former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, claimed he was paid “1.4 million” for his forthcoming memoir detailing his extraordinary backstory.Arday was dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials before he resig
entries.content:
Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, claimed he was paid “1.4 million” for his forthcoming memoir detailing his extraordinary backstory.

Arday was dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials before he resigned on Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.

His resignation came after Cambridge announced it would launch an investigation following “new information” about his qualifications and career.

Despite allegations against Arday, Simon & Schuster said earlier this week it was planning to go ahead with the publication of his memoir on 11 August in the US and 27 August in the UK. Simon & Schuster US told the Guardian on Thursday night it was “proceeding with the publication of Great and Unfortunate Things by Jason Arday as planned”.

In a previous interview with the Guardian, Arday said Simon & Schuster had offered 1.4m for the book in a “pre-empt”, a type of deal in which a publisher is so keen on a book they put in a high offer to take it off the table before it can go to auction. Arday did not specify whether the 1.4m figure was in pound sterling or US dollars. Simon & Schuster did not respond to a request to comment on the sum.

While it is a high figure, publishing sources said it would be plausible if Simon & Schuster US and UK teamed up to buy the book and sought worldwide rights – meaning they could sell the book into other regions as well as the UK and US. After the deal was signed, it was rumoured to be a seven-figure sum.

One senior publisher said it was an utterly mad number, but that “madness sometimes happens”, so it was conceivable. They said a book such as Arday’s would normally be expected to sell about 5,000 copies, so with £2 of royalty per copy, that equates to an advance of £10,000, not 1.4 million dollars or pounds.

The book recounts the story of Arday’s life, from being diagnosed with autism and global developmental delay aged three, to speaking his first words “months before starting secondary school”. In it he claims to have learned to read and write aged 18, before ultimately becoming the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge at 37.

Arday has been at the centre of a media storm since late July, when the Telegraph reported that more than 100 passages of his PhD had similarities to a thesis published six years earlier.

Doubts have been raised about claims Arday has made about prodigious fundraising feats and a Guardian investigation raised questions about his claims to have been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders and sent a pig’s head.

Cambridge initially came to Arday’s defence, describing the claims as part of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”. It said it had passed complaints on to Liverpool John Moores University, where Arday had completed his PhD. LJMU cleared him of plagiarism, but academics said legitimate concerns remained.

On Wednesday, it also emerged that Arday had appeared to have falsely claimed to have published a book titled Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse. While Palgrave Macmillan accepted the book’s proposal, it did not go ahead with publishing it, reported the Telegraph.

One publishing executive said Simon & Schuster’s decision to stand by its author thus far may simply be because “they had a contract, and they’re sticking with the contract”.

If there was a significant advance involved, there may be more motivation on the publisher’s side to “recoup” it, they added.

There have been suggestions that the publisher had to amend elements of Arday’s work. The journalist Benjamin Ryan shared a series of screenshots on social media of different versions of the memoir’s manuscript suggesting that edits had been made to dilute claims related to Arday’s fundraising efforts. Ryan has written pieces on Arday for the Washington Free Beacon, the conservative outlet behind the investigations that led to the Black academic Claudine Gay’s resignation from Harvard. Simon & Schuster did not respond when asked why these edits were made.

Pulling the book at this point would be a “pretty massive decision”, one publisher said, if only for logistical reasons: Simon & Schuster has “probably printed the book already, probably paid the author, and may have started shipping the book all over the world”, so “actively withdrawing the book now is both extremely difficult and quite expensive”.

In a statement before Arday’s resignation, Simon & Schuster said: “We have worked closely with Professor Jason Arday on Great and Unfortunate Things since acquiring it and can speak to the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication.

“Great and Unfortunate Things is Arday’s memoir of overcoming remarkable challenges and responding to adversity with resilience. It is told through his own recollections and those of the people closest to him.”

Arday “worked closely with his co-writer, as well as our editorial and legal teams, to carefully research, write and corroborate the narrative”, they added. The book is co-written by Eve Claxton.

In comments reported by the Bookseller in April, Kris Doyle, the nonfiction publisher at Simon & Schuster UK, said: “I can promise you’ve never read a story like this – even the viral news headlines don’t do it justice.”

Doyle acquired rights to publish the book in the UK and Commonwealth, while Dawn Davis, the publisher of Simon & Schuster’s 37 Ink imprint in the US, simultaneously acquired world rights. Neither Doyle nor Davis responded to questions over why Simon & Schuster had decided to pursue publication notwithstanding the controversy.

When asked to share information about the book’s fact-checking process, Simon & Schuster said: “We do not comment on our editorial processes.” In the acknowledgements section of the book, Arday credits Iman M’Fah-Traoré with checking the book. The publisher did not respond when asked whether it had contracted Traoré rather than Arday hiring her independently.

Arday is scheduled to speak in September at the Topping bookshop in Edinburgh and at Stroud book festival in November, neither of which responded when asked whether these events would go ahead.

Asked whether he would be speaking anywhere else, Simon & Schuster said they “have some additional events planned but these would all follow in the autumn so not listed as yet”. The US branch of the publisher said no official US tour was planned.

The problem facing Simon & Schuster has echoes of that faced by Penguin following the infamous Salt Path scandal, where Raynor and Moth Winn were accused of fabricating large chunks of their story.

In that case, the next book by Raynor Winn, the fourth in her bestselling series, seems to be indefinitely delayed (it’s currently scheduled for January 2028). There are clear differences between the cases – critics took issue with the accuracy of The Salt Path itself, which was marketed as an “unflinchingly honest” text, while Arday’s most-contested claims do not appear in his book.

Signing a contract for a memoir, writers promise that they have the “right to tell the story and that it’s true”, one British publisher said. Any publishing house was “relying on that warranty”.

entries.title: Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks review – an ambitious, lyrical portrait of trauma
entries.summary: A young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire RushThe world of Sky City never quite settles beneath your feet. entries.content:
The world of Sky City never quite settles beneath your feet. The action of Jacqueline Crooks’s second novel unfolds in a recognisable 1990s London, yet everything seems subtly untethered from reality: a council estate suspended above the city, voices drifting in and out through pirate radio, ghosts walking beside the living. The narrative floats just above the surface of the everyday, a world where trauma transforms the mundane into something uncanny.

We first meet protagonist Jaycee as a child, trapped in a west London housing estate she calls the Cyborg House. Her stepfather subjects her to horrific sexual abuse while her mother turns a blind eye, exercising her own brand of cruelty. Families, Jaycee comes to believe, are “dangerous places … like nests of poisonous spiders, huddled in dark, undisturbed corners, their venom, a single drop enough to rot the body inside out”. Eventually taken into care, she finds an unlikely lifeline in Ella-G, another damaged girl whose exuberance masks wounds as profound as Jaycee’s own; both feel “on the outside of the world”. The care home turns out to be similarly brutal, and the pair survive together, forging a friendship that becomes the novel’s emotional anchor.

As adults, Jaycee and Ella-G could hardly seem more different. Jaycee retreats into solitude in her high-rise council flat in Sky City, an estate perched above a shopping centre in north London where Crooks herself once lived. “Being alone is what it means to be at peace,” she tells herself. In a near-perennial state of dissociation, she imagines herself transformed by trauma into something less than fully human. Ella-G, meanwhile, propelled by her restless charisma, heads to the bright lights of New York’s music scene.

Through a conversation between past and present, Jaycee’s childhood seeps into the contemporary narrative in shards of memory and recurring visions, her adult life continually interrupted by the child she once was. Crooks sketches this psychic dislocation with extraordinary imaginative force. The abuse reverberates through Jaycee’s consciousness in fragments. She is haunted by Obsidia, a spectral child who comes to represent a version of herself.

The present-day narrative gathers momentum when Jaycee unexpectedly reconnects with Sol, a boy who offered her a rare glimpse of tenderness at secondary school before circumstance tore them apart. Their reunion carries the promise of romance, yet Crooks is after something more subtle than a conventional love story. Sol becomes another lost soul searching for belonging, his own fractured identity mirroring Jaycee’s.

As in her 2023 Women’s prize-shortlisted debut, Fire Rush, music provides the novel’s connective tissue and emotional scaffolding. An obscure blues record by a forgotten singer draws Jaycee into a quest that eventually takes her and Ella-G to Atlantic City in the search for a missing father, which becomes inseparable from Jaycee’s search for self.

Crooks’s prose, too, is deeply musical. Sentences swell and eddy in a dreamlike, rhythmic fashion, looping back on to recurring images before resolving into clarity. It takes a while to acclimatise, and at times the lyricism threatens to overwhelm the narrative. The novel’s momentum can sag beneath the weight of its own poetic ambition.

Sky City is also unapologetically bleak: there is a near constant effluvium of loneliness, hanging over the novel like the weather. Much of the narrative, as Crooks notes in the acknowledgments, is autobiographical. It feels as though she is refusing to soften or redeem her trauma for the reader’s comfort. It is a reminder that adversity can be an enduring condition, not a narrative device on the way to catharsis.

Fire Rush announced a singular literary talent: a novelist capable of fusing the propulsive rhythms of dub music with the spiritual inheritance of African spiritualism, defying conventional realism. Sky City is, in many ways, even more ambitious. It is a haunting, polyphonic meditation on trauma and belonging that hovers between realism and dream, asking how a person might rebuild a self after childhood has shattered it.

entries.title: Thirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journey

entries.content:
A memoir chronicling the comic and broadcaster John Robins’s life in alcohol and his subsequent path to sobriety, Thirst is structured around the drinks that changed his life. There’s the bottle of Jacob’s Creek wine left out on a kitchen worktop which he helped himself to at the age of seven, secreting it into his orange juice, and the beer given to him at scout camp which he drank alone. There’s also his stomach-churning recreation, while on a comedy tour of Australia, of the white russians drunk by the Dude in The Big Lebowski using a gallon of milk, a litre of vodka and a bottle of Kahlua.

As an adult, Robins, who is best known for his shows on Radio X and on BBC5 Live, romanticised pubs, which he saw as places of peacefulness and refuge. He even co-hosted the podcast The Moon Under Water where he invited guests to describe their ideal pub. Robins reveals that what kept him drinking for so long was the lie that he was in control. That he could, on occasion, get through a Dry January convinced him he couldn’t be an addict, although he got a wakeup call when a GP told him to “sort your fucking life out”.

Robins is our narrator and his reading, much like his prose, is heartfelt, darkly funny, sometimes self-lacerating and full of sage advice born from bruising experience. Currently sober, he must now grapple with the depression from which alcohol was shielding him. “I can thank alcohol for trying to step in,” he notes “but remind it that its services are no longer required, that I’ll take it from here.”

Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life is available via Penguin Audio, 11hr 36min

Further listening

The Land and Its People

David Sedaris, Little, Brown, 7hr 26min

The latest essay collection from the humorist was recorded live in front of an audience in Massachusetts and features reflections on his late mother, an anti-Trump protest in New Hampshire and the trials of looking after his partner, Hugh, after a hip operation.

The Book of Records

Madeleine Thien, Granta, 13hr 50min

Richard Lam, Athena Karkanis and Scott Turner Schofield are among the narrators of the fourth novel from the Dogs at the Perimeter author. It sees an ailing father and his daughter reflect on their past as they arrive at a remote migratory outpost called “the sea”.
